lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: Roll one die. Before it lands, write down everything that could happen: one, two, three, four, five, six.

lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: That list is called the sample space, and the whole subject rests on it.

lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: Now pick the thing you care about, say rolling a six. That is one item out of the list of six.

lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: So the probability is one out of six. The part, divided by the whole.

lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: Rolling an even number is three items out of six, so one half.

lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: Something that cannot happen, like rolling a seven, is none of the list, which is zero.

lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: Something that must happen, like rolling a number from one to six, is the whole list, which is one.

lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: So every probability lives on a line from zero to one, and that is not a rule someone decided.

lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: A part can never be bigger than the whole, or smaller than nothing.

lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: There is one condition hiding in that division, and almost every mistake in probability breaks it.

lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: The items in the list have to be equally likely.

lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: Roll two dice and add them. The totals run from two to twelve, which is eleven different answers.

lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: So is a total of seven one chance in eleven?

lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: It is tempting, and it is wrong. Eleven is a list of answers, not a list of equally likely outcomes.

lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: Paint one die red and the other blue. The red die can land six ways, and for each of those the blue die can land six ways.

lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: That is a grid of thirty-six squares, and every square is exactly as likely as every other one.

lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: Now look for the sevens. One and six, two and five, three and four, and each of those the other way round.

lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: Six squares out of thirty-six, so one in six.

lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: And a total of twelve? Only one square, six and six. One in thirty-six.

lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: Seven is six times as likely as twelve, even though both were just one item on the list of totals.

lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: Researchers who study how people learn probability have a name for this: the equiprobability bias, treating every answer as if it were equally likely.

lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: It is the most common mistake students make, and one study found that more statistics classes did not cure it. It got stronger.

lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: So here is the first answer, in one line.

lines.act: ACT ONE — A probability is a count
lines.text: A probability is a count of what you want, divided by a count of everything that could happen, and both counts have to be made of equally likely pieces.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: Now we can look at the gambler's rule with fresh eyes.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: One roll gives a six with probability one sixth. He said four rolls give four times that, four sixths.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: Let us test the rule where it cannot hide. What about seven rolls?

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: Seven times one sixth is seven sixths, more than one. A probability bigger than certain.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: The rule breaks the line from zero to one, so it was never right, even when it happened to sound close.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: Here is what adding does wrong. Adding one sixth for each roll counts every roll where a six appears.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: But a game with a six on the first roll and another six on the third roll gets counted twice.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: Adding works only when the cases cannot happen together, and sixes on different rolls can.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: So counting what we want directly is messy. A six on the first roll, or the second, or both, or three of them.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: Let us count the opposite instead.

lines.section: Count what you do not want
lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: The opposite of "at least one six" is "no six at all", and that is one single, clean case.

lines.section: Count what you do not want
lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: One roll misses the six with probability five sixths.

lines.section: Count what you do not want
lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: Four rolls all miss when the first misses, and the second, and the third, and the fourth.

lines.section: Count what you do not want
lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: Each roll does not care about the others, so the chances multiply: five sixths, four times over.

lines.section: Count what you do not want
lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: That is six hundred twenty-five out of one thousand two hundred ninety-six.

lines.section: Count what you do not want
lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: So at least one six is everything else: six hundred seventy-one out of one thousand two hundred ninety-six, fifty-one point eight percent.

lines.section: Count what you do not want
lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: Those two numbers, six hundred seventy-one and six hundred twenty-five, are written in Pascal's own letter to Fermat, dated the twenty-ninth of July, sixteen fifty-four.

lines.section: Count what you do not want
lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: The first bet really was a good bet.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: Now the double six, with exactly the same move.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: One roll of two dice misses the double six in thirty-five squares out of thirty-six.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: Twenty-four rolls all miss with probability thirty-five thirty-sixths, multiplied by itself twenty-four times.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: That comes out just over a half, fifty point nine percent.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: So at least one double six is forty-nine point one percent. Just under even. A bet that loses, slowly.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: Add one more roll, twenty-five instead of twenty-four, and it crosses to fifty point six.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: According to Pascal's letter, the gambler was so upset that he declared arithmetic had contradicted itself.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: It had not. His adding rule had.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: One honest note. Historians doubt he could have felt the difference just by playing.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: To be fairly sure that forty-nine point one is not fifty, you would need around thirteen thousand games.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: What we know for certain is the reasoning, because Pascal wrote it down.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: So that is the second answer.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: Our instinct counts answers instead of equally likely outcomes, and it adds chances that can happen together.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: Both mistakes feel natural because the wrong number is often close to the right one.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Why instinct counts the wrong thing
lines.text: Four sixths is sixty-seven percent, the truth is fifty-two. Close enough to believe, wrong enough to lose money.

lines.section: Move one: list equally likely outcomes
lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: So how do you solve a probability problem without guessing?

lines.section: Move one: list equally likely outcomes
lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: Pascal and Fermat had no formulas to look up. They had counting, and five moves cover almost everything you will meet.

lines.section: Move one: list equally likely outcomes
lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: Move one. Before you calculate anything, draw the list.

lines.section: Move one: list equally likely outcomes
lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: A grid when there are two things at once, like two dice. A tree when things happen one after another.

lines.section: Move one: list equally likely outcomes
lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: Then ask the question the gambler never asked: are these outcomes equally likely?

lines.section: Move two: "at least one" means count the opposite
lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: Move two. Whenever a question says "at least one", count "none" instead and subtract from one.

lines.section: Move two: "at least one" means count the opposite
lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: "At least one" spreads over many cases. "None" is one case.

lines.section: Move two: "at least one" means count the opposite
lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: Three coins, at least one head? There is exactly one way to get no heads, tails three times, one in eight.

lines.section: Move two: "at least one" means count the opposite
lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: So the answer is seven in eight, without listing the other seven.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: Move three. Walk down the tree. "And" means multiply along a path. "Or" means add separate paths, but only if they cannot both happen.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: A bag holds three red marbles and two blue. Draw two without putting the first back. What is the chance both are red?

lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: The first is red three times in five. Now the bag holds two red out of four, so the second is red two times in four.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: Red and then red: three fifths times two quarters, three tenths.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: Notice the second branch changed, because the first marble left the bag. The tree shows that. A formula you half-remember does not.

lines.section: Move four: turn percentages into people
lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: Move four. When the numbers are percentages, turn them into people.

lines.section: Move four: turn percentages into people
lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: A test for a rare disease is ninety-nine percent accurate, and one person in a thousand has the disease. You test positive. How worried should you be?

lines.section: Move four: turn percentages into people
lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: Most people say ninety-nine percent.

lines.section: Move four: turn percentages into people
lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: Imagine a thousand people. One of them is sick, and the test catches them.

lines.section: Move four: turn percentages into people
lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: Of the nine hundred ninety-nine who are healthy, one percent still test positive. That is about ten people.

lines.section: Move four: turn percentages into people
lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: So eleven people test positive, and only one of them is sick. About nine percent, not ninety-nine.

lines.section: Move four: turn percentages into people
lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: Psychologists have measured this. The same question, asked in people instead of percentages, gets the right answer far more often.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: Move five. Check before you trust it.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: The answer has to sit between zero and one. All the branches leaving one point of a tree must add up to one.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: And make a rough guess first. If the calculation lands far from your guess, one of them is telling you something.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Five moves for any probability problem
lines.text: The seven-sixths answer would have failed this check in one second.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — Putting it together
lines.text: A probability is a count of what you want over a count of everything that could happen, made of equally likely pieces.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — Putting it together
lines.text: Our instinct goes wrong by counting answers instead of outcomes, and by adding chances that overlap.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — Putting it together
lines.text: And five moves fix that: list, flip "at least one", multiply along "and", turn percentages into people, and check.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — Putting it together
lines.text: With those, the gambler's two bets take one line each.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — Putting it together
lines.text: One minus five sixths to the fourth: fifty-one point eight. One minus thirty-five thirty-sixths to the twenty-fourth: forty-nine point one.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — Putting it together
lines.text: Here is one to try on your own. In a room of twenty-three people, what is the chance that two of them share a birthday?

lines.act: ACT FOUR — Putting it together
lines.text: Use move two. The answer is just over half.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — Putting it together
lines.text: But Pascal and Fermat left one question open, and it is stranger than it sounds.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — Putting it together
lines.text: When we say a coin is fifty percent heads, what is that fifty percent actually describing? The coin, or you?

lines.act: ACT FOUR — Putting it together
lines.text: That is the next video, and it is waiting for you right here.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — Putting it together
lines.text: Thanks for watching, and I will see you there.
